This paper studies an important and timely problem: how a user can determine whether a black-box LLM API is actually serving the same distribution as a claimed reference model. The paper formalizes this as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem, proposes MMD-based tests with string kernels, argues that a simple Hamming kernel is especially effective in the low-sample regime, and then applies the method to commercial APIs serving Llama-family models. The empirical headline is striking: in their audit, 11 of 31 endpoints appear statistically distinguishable from Meta reference weights. Overall, I found the paper interesting, practically relevant, and likely to stimulate follow-up work. The framing is compelling, the methodology is mostly sound, and the API audit case study is valuable. At the same time, there are several methodological and interpretational issues that should be clarified before I would consider the paper fully convincing at top-tier conference standards.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the problem formulation. “Model Equality Testing” is a clean abstraction that unifies several practical concerns: provider-side modifications, silent model drift over time, and model substitution. Casting these as two-sample testing over prompt-completion pairs is natural and useful. I also appreciate that the paper explicitly targets the sampling regime rather than only greedy decoding or benchmark accuracy. This is a meaningful contribution because many real users care about the full output distribution, not just top-1 behavior. The paper also does a good job motivating why classical benchmark auditing is insufficient for long-form generation and custom prompt distributions.

The methodological choice of MMD is sensible. Kernel two-sample tests are a natural fit when one wants to compare structured outputs without log-probability access. The decomposition induced by the kernel choice, especially the prompt-matching kernel of the form 1{x=x’} times a completion kernel, is intuitive and aligns with the conditional-generation setting. The empirical finding that a simple Hamming kernel outperforms more “universal” alternatives in the small-sample regime is plausible and useful. In particular, the paper makes a good practical point: in very high-dimensional discrete spaces, universal kernels or exact-match statistics can be too sparse to be useful, whereas a coarse but informative similarity notion can yield much higher power.

The empirical scope is also a strength. The paper does not stop at synthetic perturbations; it evaluates quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps, and then real commercial endpoints. The API audit is the most compelling part of the paper. Even if some readers may debate the exact interpretation of a rejection, the fact that a lightweight statistical procedure can repeatedly detect differences across providers is noteworthy. The release of code and a large completion dataset further increases the paper’s practical value.

That said, my main concern is that the paper sometimes overstates what its test establishes. The title and framing suggest identifying “which model” an API is serving, but the actual statistical object is much weaker: detecting whether the sampled distribution differs from one or two chosen references under a specific prompt distribution, decoding setup, and output representation. A rejection does not identify the cause of the difference, nor does non-rejection establish equality except relative to the test’s power. The paper usually acknowledges this in the technical sections, but some of the broader claims and presentation risk stronger interpretations than are warranted. In particular, statements like an endpoint “serves a different distribution than reference weights” are technically correct only relative to the tested prompt distribution, temperature, truncation length, and character/token representation. I would strongly encourage the authors to sharpen this language throughout, especially in the abstract and conclusions.

A second major issue is the dependence of the result on prompt distribution and decoding configuration. The paper defines equality relative to a prompt distribution pi and maximum length L, which is appropriate, but this means the test is not assessing global model equality. In practice, the audit conclusions may vary substantially with prompt set, prompt language, task type, temperature, top-p, stop sequences, system prompts, and provider-specific defaults. The paper partially addresses this by using multiple prompt distributions and by explicitly requesting temperature 1, but the robustness analysis is still limited. For example, many APIs implement temperature, top-p, repetition penalties, or stop handling differently, and these differences alone could induce rejection even if the underlying weights are identical. That may still be useful from a user perspective, but then the paper is auditing endpoint behavior rather than model identity. I think the paper should foreground this distinction more clearly and perhaps rename some claims accordingly.

Relatedly, the commercial audit section raises several confounding concerns. The paper compares API outputs to local reference weights from Hugging Face, but many implementation details besides weights can differ: tokenizer version, chat template, BOS/EOS handling, system prompt insertion, safety filters, stop-token behavior, max-token truncation, speculative decoding artifacts, caching, and undocumented sampling defaults. Some providers may also canonicalize prompts or apply moderation layers. The paper interprets rejections as evidence of “modified distributions,” which is fair, but some passages imply stronger conclusions about quantization or substitution. Without tighter control over endpoint configuration, it is difficult to attribute the source of the discrepancy. This does not invalidate the audit, but it does limit causal interpretation. The paper would benefit from a more systematic discussion of these confounds and, ideally, ablations showing how much rejection can be induced by known benign implementation mismatches.

I also have concerns about the statistical protocol used in the API audit. The paper says tests are conducted at level alpha = 0.01 using N = 10m samples, then repeated over ten samples, and endpoints “fail” if the average rejection rate is at least 0.5. This is not a standard hypothesis-testing procedure, and it is not obvious what overall Type I error guarantee this meta-decision rule enjoys. The paper carefully argues Type I control for the composite null when combining the two null references with an AND rule, but I did not see a corresponding justification for the repeated-testing-and-thresholding procedure. If each replicate is a valid level-0.01 test, then thresholding the empirical rejection rate across ten runs changes the operating characteristics in a nontrivial way. It may reduce false positives, but the paper should either derive or empirically calibrate the resulting error rate. As written, the audit section mixes formal testing language with an ad hoc stability heuristic. This is fixable, but it needs clarification.

A related point is multiple testing. The paper audits many endpoints across multiple prompt distributions and sometimes combines results with Bonferroni correction in a figure, but the main table appears to report per-task failures without a unified family-wise or false discovery control across all 31 endpoints and tasks. Since the paper’s headline result is “11 out of 31 endpoints,” the exact multiplicity correction matters. If the authors want to make endpoint-level claims across several prompt distributions, they should define the family of hypotheses and the correction procedure precisely. Otherwise, readers may overinterpret the count of flagged endpoints.

On the methodological side, the Hamming kernel is practical, but the paper could do more to explain when it should or should not work. Since it is only a pseudometric, there are many distributional changes it cannot detect. The fp16 result already hints at this. More broadly, Hamming similarity on decoded strings may be sensitive to superficial lexical or formatting changes while missing semantic shifts that preserve token overlap. Conversely, it may detect harmless stylistic differences that matter little for downstream use. The paper briefly notes that kernel choice determines semantics, but this is actually central. I would like to see a more explicit characterization of the alternatives to which the Hamming MMD is most sensitive, perhaps via controlled perturbation studies: synonym substitution, formatting changes, safety preambles, deterministic post-processing, or semantic-preserving paraphrases. This would help users understand what a rejection means.

The comparison to alternative tests is useful but somewhat incomplete. The paper compares against one-hot MMD, all-substrings MMD, and two multinomial tests. However, there are other natural baselines in this setting: embedding-based distances over completions, edit-distance kernels, n-gram feature MMD, classifier two-sample tests, energy distance on learned representations, or tests based on next-token logprob access when available. Since the paper’s main claim is that Hamming MMD is especially powerful and sample-efficient, stronger baselines would make that claim more convincing. In particular, a classifier two-sample test on simple text features or embeddings could be a strong practical competitor.

I also found some aspects of the simulation setup somewhat narrow. The main prompt distribution in Section 4 is a uniform distribution over random 100-character Wikipedia strings in five languages, with continuation prompts. This is a reasonable stress test for long-form generation, but it is not obvious that it reflects the kinds of prompts where provider modifications matter most. The paper later includes HumanEval and UltraChat in the API audit, which helps, but the kernel-selection conclusions are still largely based on the Wikipedia continuation task. It would strengthen the paper to show that the Hamming kernel remains preferable across a broader range of prompt styles, especially instruction-following prompts with stronger formatting regularities.

The finetuning experiment is interesting, but I would be cautious about the interpretation. Detecting finetuning after a small number of steps on a 1000-example dataset is plausible, but the paper seems to suggest a broader conclusion that full finetuning is hard to localize and therefore relevant to unlearning or model editing. That extrapolation feels too strong from the presented evidence. The experiment only shows detectability on one evaluation distribution for one model and two finetuning datasets. It is a nice demonstration, but not enough to support broader claims about the impossibility of localized changes.

The distance-estimation results are intriguing, especially the clustering by model family, but they should be presented more carefully. Since the Hamming MMD is not a true metric on distributions, interpreting absolute values as “distance” can be misleading. The paper does mention pseudometric status, but then uses language like “further from the reference than an entirely different language model,” which sounds stronger than justified. This is directionally informative, but the authors should be careful not to overstate the geometric meaning of these numbers.

There are also some reproducibility and implementation details that deserve more attention. For API comparisons, were prompts sent through identical chat templates across providers? Were providers instructed with raw text completion endpoints or chat endpoints? How were stop sequences handled? Were outputs normalized before character-level comparison, for example with respect to Unicode normalization, whitespace, or provider-added prefixes? Were rate limits, retries, or caching effects controlled? Since small formatting differences can matter for a Hamming-style statistic, these details are important. The paper references appendices for some details, but the main text should summarize the most consequential controls.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has substantial merit. The core idea is useful, the empirical findings are interesting, and the work opens a valuable line of inquiry around black-box model auditing. My overall assessment is positive but not unreservedly so. I would lean toward acceptance if the venue values practical auditing methods and empirical systems-oriented ML work, but I would want the final version to tighten its claims and clarify the statistical protocol.

The most important revisions I would request are the following. First, clearly distinguish endpoint-behavior equality from underlying-weight equality, and avoid language that implies stronger identification than the test supports. Second, provide a formal or empirical justification for the repeated-audit decision rule used in the API study, including its effective false positive rate. Third, clarify multiplicity handling for the headline endpoint counts. Fourth, expand discussion of confounds in commercial API comparisons and, if possible, add controls or ablations for common implementation mismatches. Fifth, broaden or strengthen baselines for the kernel/test comparison. Sixth, better characterize the sensitivity profile of the Hamming kernel so users understand what kinds of changes it detects.

If these issues are addressed, I believe the paper could make a meaningful contribution. It identifies a real problem, proposes a practical framework, and demonstrates that black-box API auditing can be done statistically and cheaply. Even where I am skeptical, I think the paper is asking the right question, and that alone makes it valuable.

My recommendation is a weak accept to borderline accept, contingent on stronger clarification of claims and statistical methodology.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper formalizes auditing black-box LLM APIs as a two-sample hypothesis testing problem called Model Equality Testing. Given samples from a reference model and an API, it applies MMD-based kernel tests to determine whether the output distributions differ under a prompt distribution of interest. The main methodological proposal is to use a simple Hamming string kernel over completions, motivated by sample efficiency in high-dimensional output spaces. Through simulations on quantization, watermarking, finetuning, and model substitution, the paper reports that the Hamming-MMD test has substantially higher power than several alternatives in low-sample regimes. It then audits 31 commercial endpoints serving Llama models and reports that 11 endpoints appear statistically different from Meta reference weights. The paper also uses estimated MMD values as an effect-size notion to compare models and providers.
strengths: Timely and practically important problem: users increasingly rely on black-box LLM APIs and need tools to detect undocumented model changes or substitutions.
Clear problem formulation as a conditional two-sample testing task over prompt-completion pairs, which is conceptually clean and broadly applicable.
Method is simple, computationally feasible, and easy to deploy in practice; the use of a Hamming kernel is intuitive and appears effective in low-sample settings.
Strong empirical breadth: evaluates quantization, watermarking, finetuning, model swaps, and real commercial APIs across multiple providers and model variants.
Includes comparisons against several baselines, including one-hot/all-substrings kernels and multinomial closeness tests, which helps justify the proposed choice.
Practical contribution is significant: open-sourced code and a large dataset of completions improve reproducibility and downstream use.
The API audit case study is compelling and likely to be of broad interest to the community.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is somewhat limited: the main contribution is selecting and validating a particular kernelized MMD instantiation rather than introducing a fundamentally new testing framework.

The empirical setup may conflate many sources of variation beyond model identity, including tokenizer differences, prompt formatting, system prompts, stop conditions, safety filters, server-side decoding details, and undocumented preprocessing/postprocessing by providers.

The proposed Hamming kernel is only a pseudometric and is not characteristic/universal, so the test can systematically miss distribution shifts that do not manifest as position-wise token/character agreement differences.

The paper emphasizes power but provides limited calibration evidence on Type-I error in the exact regimes used for API auditing, especially under character-space comparisons and repeated testing/aggregation heuristics.

The real-world audit conclusions are strong, but causal attribution is weak: rejecting equality does not identify whether the cause is quantization, watermarking, prompt templating, decoding mismatch, safety intervention, or a different base model.
The prompt distributions used in simulation are relatively narrow and synthetic (e.g., random Wikipedia continuations), which may limit claims of generality to realistic downstream applications.

The decision rule for endpoint failure (average rejection rate over ten repeats >= 0.5) is heuristic and not tied to a formal hypothesis-testing guarantee for the final reported endpoint-level conclusions.
methodological_flaws: The composite-null testing procedure in Section 5 controls false positives for the conjunction rule p1<alpha AND p2<alpha for a single trial, but the paper's final endpoint decision is based on repeating tests ten times and thresholding the average rejection rate at 0.5. No formal error-rate control is provided for this aggregated procedure, so the reported endpoint failure labels are not backed by the same statistical guarantee as the base test.

The paper claims broad auditing of whether an API serves the same model distribution, but equality is tested in character space for APIs while references are sampled locally. Character-space comparison can introduce artifacts unrelated to model distribution, such as Unicode normalization, whitespace handling, truncation, hidden templates, or detokenization differences. This weakens the scientific validity of interpreting rejection as model modification.

The Hamming kernel is not characteristic, so MMD=0 does not imply equality. While acknowledged, the paper sometimes frames the method as testing model equality in general terms. Strictly speaking, with this kernel the test is only guaranteed to detect differences visible through the chosen feature map, not all distributional differences.

Power estimates are based on only 100 Monte Carlo simulations, which can yield fairly noisy estimates, especially when comparing methods with modest differences. The paper reports medians and trends but gives limited uncertainty quantification for many headline claims.

The simulation-based p-value computation assumes faithful sampling from the null reference distribution P. In practice, local reference inference may itself differ due to implementation details (hardware kernels, sampling library behavior, seed handling, tokenizer/version mismatches), and the paper does not fully quantify how robust the test is to such reference-side misspecification.

The empirical comparisons may not be entirely fair across kernels/tests because the Hamming kernel exploits structured similarity while multinomial baselines operate on exact collisions in an enormous space; stronger structured baselines or learned embeddings are not explored, so the conclusion that Hamming-MMD is best may be incomplete.

The correlation analysis between MMD and HumanEval accuracy difference is descriptive only and based on pairwise comparisons with shared endpoints/models, so the reported R^2 should not be overinterpreted as validating MMD as a proxy for capability differences.
